translations: The morning mist had barely cleared when the pier at Chen Tang Pass was already packed with people. Nets lay on the stone steps, drying, their damp knots dripping water that seeped into the gaps between the green bricks, leaving a small patch of dark stain. Old Zhang, the salted fish seller, squatted on the ground, cracking his knuckles as he counted his money, his nails dusted with fish scales. He looked up and saw the old woman next door, carrying an empty basket, scolding a chicken—she’d stolen her sun‑dried shrimp yesterday, and this morning the chicken had flown into the temple roof eaves to play hide‑and‑seek. Nezha, barefoot, wiped sweat from his forehead on the threshold, clutching a half‑cool sesame cake; crumbs fell off in a fine dust. Li Jing sat in the courtyard sharpening arrows; sparks from the iron made his cuffs shine. Suddenly a thud rang from the wall, and he looked up to see his son leaning his neck to drink from a well, his Adam’s apple rolling twice before he wiped his mouth and said, “Dad, this water is sweet!”

“Sweet? That’s just the sugar syrup from your mother’s pickled plums seeping into the well wall.” Lady Yin, carrying a dustpan, passed by with a basket of freshly snapped bean sprouts. “Besides, even if it’s sweet, it’s not meant to be eaten as a meal.”

Nezha licked the crumbs off his lip, turned, and ran toward the alley’s mouth, his skirt brushing a string of wind‑chime grass that tinkled a few times. At that moment Aman, carrying an old cloth bag, stumbled in, nearly dropping a green bamboo slip from his arms. He knelt on one knee, scooped up the slip, and brushed off the dust. The more he brushed, the more dust fell—he’d just waded through a muddy puddle, his trouser legs soaked with dampness, and a shake sent a miniature rain. “Ouch!” he shrank his neck to avoid the spray, holding his pen in his mouth, and muttered, “The ‘Twenty Bamboo Slips of Mountains and Seas’ has opened another blank page! Kids, don’t kick the sand; I just wrote ‘the cooking smoke leans but doesn’t stir!’”

Nezha bent down, picked up a pebble the size of a marble, and gently tossed it onto the water. Ripples spread, startling two white egrets. “You say people by the sea deal with waves every day—how can they not get annoyed?”

Aman steadied his crooked bamboo hat, pulled out an old, bald pen, dipped it in saliva, and wrote, “Because annoyance is annoyance, you still have to steam rice, mend nets, and soothe the kids to sleep—look, over there under the old locust tree, three kids are doing a human pyramid to get at a bird’s nest; the first one who falls cries, the second one laughs right after.”
Li Jing set down his file, glanced toward the direction where the city tower’s flag fluttered, and suddenly said, “The sea is so quiet today.”
Lady Yin pulled back the curtain, peeking out, her fingertips gripping a broken needle. “Quiet’s good. It keeps Nezha from pulling the mixed‑sky silk to wash his scarf again.”

Lady Yin pulled back the curtain, peeking out, her fingertips gripping a broken needle. “Quiet’s good. It keeps Nezha from pulling the mixed‑sky silk to wash his scarf again.” Hearing this, Nezha indeed tucked the freshly untied mixed‑sky silk behind his back. The red silk was too long, so it trailed from his shoulder all the way to the door, just sweeping over Old Zhang’s bamboo fish‑rack. Old Zhang chased after him, demanding an explanation. Nezha lifted the rack, still saying, “It just realized it was on the wrong path.” Li Jing glanced at him and asked, “If the silk realized it was wrong, why doesn’t your hand recognize it?” Nezha honestly hung the fish one by one back on the rack; when he reached the last one, he found it crooked, so he reached out and steadied it three times. Aman, standing nearby, wrote “Nezha helps hang fish” in his notebook. Just as he finished, Old Zhang leaned over to see, “You still need to add that he was the one who knocked it over first.” Aman had to squeeze out a line of small characters and sigh, “You Chen Tang Pass folks remember a good deed, but you also add a half‑bad one?” Lady Yin shoved a hot pancake at him, “If it weren’t a half‑bad one, this slip wouldn’t be so lively.” Aman bit into it, the heat making him gasp, but he couldn’t let go: “Lively as it is, can the pancake at least talk about some boundaries?”

Nezha lifted his eyebrows, smiled, and the red silk around his wrist twirled in the wind like an unawakened snake. He kicked off his legs and ran to the Nine Bay River bank; his soles burned, so he quickly plunged into the shallow water. The river was cool, soaking his calves; he scooped a handful and splashed it on his face, droplets running down his chin into his collar, making his shoulders raise. A willow branch hung over the shore; he casually snapped a piece off, peeled it, and wrapped it around his wrist. The mixed‑sky silk, once flat in his arm, was now damp and suddenly unfolded like a living thing; the red silk floated on the water, winding like a carp’s back. He lifted his toes, splashed water onto it, and a splash erupted, the silk’s surface instantly glowing with golden patterns—not from the sun, but from the silk itself lighting up. Nezha gasped, reached out, and the mixed‑sky silk, following his motion, wrapped his arm three times, then yanked hard! The entire Nine Bay River roared, waves swirling upward, reeds snapping and springing back as if someone had yanked their roots hard. Downstream, a flock of ducks burst into a cacophony; a green‑headed duck, panicked, rushed onto a field ridge, flapping its wings, making the rice leaves crackle. From the distant sea came a rumbling thud, not a rain drop from the sky, but a deep, heavy tremor from the ocean’s depths.
